cards.front: Why do X-rays show fractures clearly but give little detail of ligaments and tendons?
cards.back: Dense **bone** absorbs more X-ray radiation than soft tissue does, so bone shows up clearly while soft tissue gives little contrast.
cards.hint: Compare how dense each tissue is.

cards.front: Which imaging technique best shows a torn ligament?
cards.back: **MRI**, because it gives detailed images of soft tissue such as ligaments and uses no ionising radiation.
cards.hint: Think about which tissues X-rays show poorly.

cards.back: An artificial device that **replaces** a missing or damaged part of the body.
cards.hint: Think about what it does when a body part is gone.

cards.front: Why do doctors avoid repeated X-ray scans?
cards.back: X-rays use **ionising radiation**, which can damage cells, so the dose is kept as low as possible.
cards.hint: Think about what radiation does to living cells.

cards.back: An **external device** worn outside the body that supports, protects or corrects a body part.
cards.hint: Think about a part that is still there.

cards.front: A student says a knee brace is a prosthesis because it is worn on the knee. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: A brace supports a knee that is still present, so it is an **orthosis**. A prosthesis replaces a missing or damaged part.
cards.hint: Ask whether the knee has been replaced or only supported.

cards.front: What are the drawbacks of MRI scanning?
cards.back: Scans are **slower** and cost more, even though MRI uses no ionising radiation.
cards.hint: Think about time and money compared with other techniques.

cards.back: Imaging that uses **reflections** of high-frequency sound waves from boundaries between tissues to build a moving image.
cards.hint: Think about what sound does when it meets a boundary.

cards.front: How does a carbon-fibre running blade help an athlete with a lower-limb amputation?
cards.back: It replaces the missing lower limb; it bends under load and springs back, returning some of the **energy** stored in each stride.
cards.hint: Think about what the blade does when the foot lands.

cards.front: Why is a prosthesis made to suit the individual?
cards.back: A **good fit** is comfortable and avoids damaging the tissue that remains.
cards.hint: Think about what the body still has after an injury.

cards.front: How can a shoe insert reduce stress on the knee?
cards.back: It corrects the way the foot lands, which **reduces stress** on the shin and knee.
cards.hint: Start with the moment the foot hits the ground.

cards.front: How can wearable sensors help prevent injury in sport?
cards.back: They record **movement and heart rate**, so coaches can spot poor technique or excessive load early.
cards.hint: Think about what a coach needs to notice before an injury.

cards.back: **Keyhole surgery** in which a camera and instruments are passed through small cuts to examine or repair a joint.
cards.hint: Compare it with a large open cut.

cards.front: How does technology help track and confirm recovery after an injury?
cards.back: Machines measure **joint movement and muscle strength** to track progress, and ultrasound or MRI checks that damaged tissue has healed.
cards.hint: Think about measuring progress first, then looking inside.
